Yellowstone County in brief

Yellowstone County had 164,731 residents in 2020, more than any other Montana county. Its seat, Billings, is also its largest city, and the Yellowstone River crosses it from southwest to northeast. Billings, Laurel and Broadview are the incorporated places, and the rest of the county is unincorporated, including communities such as Huntley, Lockwood, Shepherd and Worden.

Treat it as several markets rather than a single one, and price accordingly. A Billings neighborhood house, a farm parcel near Shepherd and a lot in Broadview use the same county offices yet sit in different school and utility districts. A home inside a city carries city levies on top of county and school levies. A home in Lockwood or Huntley is billed with its own school and special districts. Rural parcels often add well, septic and road access questions that a city lot never raises.

Because districts differ, two houses of equal value can get different tax bills, and buyers tend to compare bills first.

Who handles property tax

The Yellowstone County Treasurer bills and collects. Valuation is the Montana Department of Revenue's job. The same office issues tax deeds and tax lien assignment certificates, records miscellaneous revenue and processes tax protests and mobile home moving permits.

  • Treasurer, in person: Room 113, 2825 3rd Ave N, Billings, MT 59101
  • Treasurer, by mail: P.O. Box 35010, Billings, MT 59107
  • Treasurer, by phone: 406-256-2802
  • Tax Appeal Board: 406-256-2701, P.O. Box 35001, Billings

Look up your parcel on the county's tax records search, or read the property tax page. Each year the office collects about $345 million in real and personal property taxes across roughly 75,000 real estate bills, 5,900 mobile home bills and 1,050 personal property bills. At that volume, due dates and penalties are enforced strictly.

Due dates and penalties

Real estate tax is billed in two halves, and each is due by 5 PM Mountain Time. If the date is a weekend or holiday, you get the next business day.

Yellowstone County payment due dates
Tax typeFirst halfSecond half
Real estateNovember 30 (2026 only: December 3)May 31 (2027 only: June 1)
Mobile homeMay 31 (2027 only: June 1)November 30
Personal propertyJune 30None

Pay late and you owe a 2% penalty, then 5/6 of 1% interest for every month after. That applies equally to houses, personal property, mobile homes and farm and ranch land. The 2026 first-half deadline moved to December 3. If you close in late November or early December, find out from your title company which date it is using.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Yellowstone County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens when taxes go delinquent

The county attaches a tax lien, and a third party may then buy an assignment of it. Assignments are sold in late August, with a $50 fee for each one.

From there the process is slow, with several notices along the way. Lienholders may pay later delinquent taxes on an assigned parcel only between June 1 and July 30 (June 2 to July 30 in 2027). In the last year of the redemption period, a notice that a tax deed may be issued goes out between May 1 and May 30. A tax deed carries a $25 deed fee plus recording fees of $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page.

Lien buyers do not get legal advice from the county. If an investor now holds a lien on your house, treat it as a payoff item: the title company has to clear it, along with the lienholder's interest and costs. The county's tax lien page carries the certificate list and the rules as they stand now, which changed after recent legislation.

How to appeal your valuation

Your first move is a written objection, sent within 30 days of the date printed on the classification and appraisal notice. Do that and the appeal covers both years of the two-year cycle for residential and commercial property. The timing rules come from Montana Code Annotated sections 15-7-102 and 15-15-102:

  • Only one application for reduction is allowed per valuation cycle.
  • Miss the 30 days and the objection reaches only the second year, due by June 1 of that year.
  • Count the 30 days from the notice date rather than the day it reached you. Mailing days are not added.
  • Whether a late appeal had good cause, for example a notice sent to the wrong address, is for the County Tax Appeal Board alone to decide.

If the informal review with the Department of Revenue disappoints you, take it to the county board next, and the State Tax Appeal Board after that. A recent sale price, an independent appraisal or other market evidence all help your case. Completed forms go to the Clerk and Recorder's office.

Selling with taxes owed

Any unpaid tax comes out of the seller's proceeds when the deal closes. Your title company asks the Treasurer what is owed, penalty and monthly interest included, then pays it from the sale.

The steps look like this:

  • Get the current amount owed on your parcel from the Treasurer.
  • If a lien has been assigned to an investor, get a written payoff from the lienholder too, since its costs are added.
  • Give both figures to the title company before agreeing to a price.
  • Paying by the due date is best, since the 5/6 of 1% monthly interest keeps adding up.

A cash buyer can still close with a tax balance outstanding, because the payoff is taken from the sale. We buy houses as-is and quote a price only after seeing the property.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Yellowstone County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the Treasurer's office

A short visit goes faster with the right items. Bring the parcel number or property address, a photo ID, and the closing date if you have one. Ask whether any tax lien assignment certificate exists for the parcel, and if so, who holds it. If you plan to appeal, ask the Tax Appeal Board at 406-256-2701 which forms apply, then mail them to the Clerk and Recorder at P.O. Box 35001, Billings, MT 59101.

Mobile homes and personal property

Mobile homes and personal property keep their own calendar, shown in the table above: personal property is due June 30, and a mobile home's first half falls on May 31. If you are selling a mobile home, confirm both halves are paid before closing; the Treasurer's office can state the balance. That office also issues mobile home moving permits, so ask about one if the home will be moved off the lot. If your sale is a plain house with no mobile home or business property, you can skip this part and focus on the real estate dates above. Otherwise, add these balances to your payoff checklist so nothing is left for the buyer to discover after closing.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Yellowstone County?

The county Treasurer, at 2825 3rd Ave N, Room 113 in Billings. Call 406-256-2802. Values themselves come from the state revenue department.

When is real estate tax due in Yellowstone County?

Twice a year, on November 30 and May 31, by 5 PM Mountain Time. This year's first half is due December 3, and next year's second half is due June 1.

What is the late penalty in Yellowstone County?

The penalty is 2%, and interest runs at 5/6 of 1% every month the bill stays unpaid, whatever the property type.

How long do I have to appeal my valuation?

Thirty days from the date on the appraisal notice gets you both years of the cycle. Filing later covers only year two, and the cutoff is June 1.

Can I sell my Yellowstone County house if there is a tax lien?

Yes. Closing pays off the lien and its costs from your proceeds, so request written payoff figures from the Treasurer and any lienholder first.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Gallatin County?

Gallatin County at a glance

Bozeman is the seat of Gallatin County, which fills a corner of southwest Montana. About 118,960 people lived here in 2020, behind only one other Montana county. Bozeman, Belgrade and Three Forks are cities, Manhattan and West Yellowstone are towns, and Big Sky, Gallatin Gateway and Four Corners are among the unincorporated communities. Big Sky Resort lies partly in Gallatin and partly in Madison County.

Jobs center on Montana State University and Bozeman Health. Since 2010 few Montana counties have added people faster, and Bozeman alone is forecast at 87,400 residents, close to half of the county's projected total. New arrivals and a young population turning over around the university keep houses in demand.

Values here are high enough that many primary residences cross the $378,000 line in the 2026 rate schedule, so they pay at more than one rate.

How Gallatin County homes are taxed in 2026

What you do with the house decides the rate. Live in it and the state charges 0.76 percent up to $378,000, then 0.90 percent through $756,000, then 1.10 percent through $1,511,999, then 1.90 percent for the rest. Use it as a vacation place, a short-term rental or a vacant lot and every dollar is charged 1.90 percent. After that, mills set by your city, school district and special districts convert the taxable value into a bill.

Homestead ruleWhat Montana requires
Homestead eligibilityOwner lives there at least 7 months of the year
Long-term rental eligibilityRented 28 or more days for at least 7 months a year
Rate after a saleStays through the calendar year; new owner must apply by March 1
Eligible homesSingle-family, townhome, condo, manufactured home with up to 1 acre

Because resort areas like Big Sky are inside county lines, double-check the class your property was in before pricing it. Someone moving in will probably want to claim the homestead rate for the following year.

When Gallatin County taxes are due

Gallatin County property tax arrives as one bill with two payment dates. Half comes due at 5 p.m. on November 30, or 30 days after the postmark if your notice went out late, and the remainder at 5 p.m. on May 31. The statute behind this is Montana Code 15-16-102.

Owner-occupants can sign up for seven nearly equal monthly payments, each due on a month's last day between November 30 and May 31. A missed installment turns delinquent right away, with the usual 2 percent penalty and monthly interest. Arrears from earlier years do not prevent you from paying this year's bill, but anything earmarked for delinquency gets applied to the oldest year first.

Selling mid-year? Find out from the title company which half is paid. The unpaid half and the share belonging to each party can shift the numbers on the closing statement.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Gallatin County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who to contact

Two offices split the work. Money questions belong to the county treasurer, who sits at 311 West Main, Room 103 in Bozeman and answers at 406-582-3033 or 406-582-3030. Value and class questions belong to the state's Bozeman Office, reachable at 406-582-3400 or dorgallatinoffice@mt.gov.

  • Treasurer: tax bills, payments, delinquent taxes, tax liens and assignments.
  • Department of Revenue Bozeman Office: appraisal, classification, corrections to property characteristics.
  • Clerk and Recorder: receives direct appeals to the county tax appeal board.
  • Title company: confirms what is owed and pays it at closing.

Check that the state has your current mailing address. Notices of pending liens are mailed to whatever address is on file, and an email to the Bozeman office will update it.

Delinquent taxes and tax liens

A payment made after the due date is late immediately and picks up a 2 percent penalty, plus interest of 5/6 of 1 percent each month. Montana Code 15-17-125 requires a lien on real property that is still unpaid by the first working day in August.

The sequence runs like this. A courtesy notice goes out once the first half is late. When the second half is late, a notice appears in the Bozeman Daily Chronicle, and about two weeks before that August date pending lien notices are mailed. If nothing has been paid by August 31, an outside party may take assignment of the lien by covering all taxes, penalty, interest and costs.

Bozeman adds a twist. The city forwards delinquent special assessments to the county for collection, so an owner can have paid county property tax and still face a lien for unpaid Bozeman special assessments.

  • August 1 (first working day): liens attach to still-delinquent properties.
  • August 15: earliest date an assignee may mail the required notice of pending assignment.
  • August 31: first day assignments can be purchased.
  • September 1: most assignments are issued.

Appealing a valuation and paying under protest

The deadline is 30 days after the date on the classification and appraisal notice. In that window you can send Form AB-26 to the Department of Revenue, or bypass it and go to the county tax appeal board through the clerk and recorder. A further appeal reaches the Montana Tax Appeal Board, and its rulings stand unless district court says otherwise.

Protecting a possible refund with interest takes two things: a written protest to the county treasurer, and full payment of the disputed tax before it turns delinquent. Evidence you bring this cycle is judged as of January 1, 2024.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Gallatin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with a lien or unpaid assessments

You can still sell with a lien in place. The title company tracks down every open item, such as county tax, penalty, interest and Bozeman special assessments, and pays them out of your proceeds at closing. With a cash buyer no underwriter is waiting on a payoff letter.

Steps that help: request the treasurer's current balance early, ask whether the city has sent any special assessments to the county, and compare the final statement against both numbers before signing. If the house is rented or vacant, mention that to the buyer too, since it can affect which rate class applies from here on.

Many sellers ask whether the buyer inherits the old rate, and the answer is no, not for long. The rate class carries through the end of the calendar year, then the new owner has to apply. Passing along your last tax bill and any homestead approval gives them what they need to file. Buyers who will rent the house long term should apply too, and should plan on renting for at least seven months of the year.

Frequently asked questions

Who sets my Gallatin County property value?

The Montana Department of Revenue. The county treasurer bills the tax, and the department's Bozeman Office at 406-582-3400 answers value and classification questions.

What happens on August 1 if my taxes are unpaid?

The county treasurer attaches a tax lien to real property with delinquent taxes as of the first working day in August, and files it with the Clerk and Recorder. A copy goes to the owner's recorded address.

Can I owe Bozeman special assessments even if I paid county tax?

Yes. Bozeman forwards delinquent special assessments to the county, and they become part of the county's collection process, so a lien can attach for them.

How much is the 2026 rate on a Gallatin County second home?

A flat 1.90 percent of market value applies to second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots. A primary residence starts at 0.76 percent.

Can I sell my Gallatin County house for cash with a lien on it?

Yes. The title company pays the lien, penalty and interest from the sale proceeds at closing, and a cash buyer does not need lender approval to proceed.

Selling in Cascade County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Cascade County?
We buy Cascade County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Cascade County at a glance

Great Falls is the county seat of Cascade County and the only city in it. Belt, Cascade and Neihart are the small towns, and 84,414 people lived here at the 2020 census. Beyond town limits you find places like Black Eagle, Sand Coulee, Simms, Ulm and Vaughn. A city lot and a rural house are very different listings. Whoever buys the rural one will want to hear about the well, the septic system and how the road is plowed in January.

Malmstrom Air Force Base shapes local demand more than any other employer. Its 150 launch facilities are spread across a missile complex of 13,800 square miles, so government sites sit near many rural parcels. It has 3,896 assigned personnel (3,371 military and 525 civilian) and 1,116 privatized housing units. Many buyers and sellers here move when base assignments change, so a sale on a tight clock is common.

Selling on a short move timeline

Got orders? Give every buyer your report date at the first conversation. A buyer with a mortgage has to clear an appraisal and underwriting first. A cash buyer does neither, so closing can match your moving truck, and the house is taken as is, which spares you a round of last-minute repairs.

Property tax gets settled at closing no matter who buys. Before you list or accept an offer, collect:

  • Your latest tax statement and any protest or AB-26 paperwork.
  • Proof of homestead enrollment, if you have it.
  • The orders that set your move date, if a transfer drives the sale.

2026 tax rates on Cascade County homes

For 2026, Montana sorts homes into classes with different rates. Each bracket of value carries its own percentage. Mills from every district at your address, such as the city, the school district and special districts, are applied last. That is why identical values can produce different bills. Your tax statement shows the real number.

Property type (2026)Tax rate on market value
Lived-in home or long-term rental: value up to $378,0000.76 percent
Lived-in home or long-term rental: $378,001 to $756,0000.90 percent
Lived-in home or long-term rental: $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10 percent
Lived-in home or long-term rental: over $1,511,9991.90 percent
Vacation home, short-term rental or empty residential lot1.90 percent
Multifamily dwelling rented long term1.10 percent

The lower bracketed rate is the homestead rate. Houses, townhomes, condos and manufactured homes qualify with an acre or less of land, as long as the owner occupies the home seven months or more.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Cascade County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead rate when you sell

Your homestead status is not a permanent feature of the house. After a sale, the approved rate rides along until December 31 of that year. The next owner then has to file an application of their own, and for tax year 2027 the enrollment window ends March 1, 2027.

Landlords who buy have their own path. A rental earns the bracketed rate if tenants stay 28 days or more and the house is rented at least seven months of the year, but the owner must still apply in the window. Skip the form, or switch to short stays, and the 1.90 percent flat rate applies.

  • Seller: hand the title company your last tax bill and homestead approval.
  • Owner-occupant buyer: file the homestead application before March 1.
  • Long-term landlord buyer: apply during the rental window and plan on seven months of qualifying tenancy.

Due dates and penalties

Cascade County bills in two installments. Pay the first by 5 p.m. on November 30, unless your notice was postmarked late, in which case you get thirty days from the postmark. Pay the second by 5 p.m. on May 31. Montana Code 15-16-102 is the authority. Weekend and holiday deadlines roll to the following business day, still at 5 p.m.

Owners who live in the house can choose seven equal installments instead, due on the final day of every month from November through May (the dates run November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31). Cascade County's treasurer lists two payment plans, and this is the one for real estate. Enrollment goes through the treasurer's office.

Late payment costs a 2 percent penalty plus monthly interest of 5/6 of 1 percent. Old arrears cannot stop you from paying the current year. Money aimed at delinquency, however, lands on the oldest year first, and settling this year leaves an earlier year's lien untouched.

Disputing your valuation

If the number looks wrong, take it up with the state agency that set it, the Department of Revenue, rather than the treasurer. The clock is 30 days from the date on the classification and appraisal notice. Within that time you can mail Form AB-26 for an informal look, or go directly to the county clerk and recorder and ask for a county tax appeal board hearing.

This cycle's values are fixed as of January 1, 2024, so build your case around that date. Proof that helps: your own estimate of value, a purchase price from within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales and listings, and a builder's cost breakdown if you remodeled. Start by checking square footage and room counts on Property.MT.gov, then phone your Department of Revenue field office to talk it through with an appraiser.

If the informal answer disappoints you, the next stop is the county tax appeal board, which county commissioners appoint and which operates independently. After that come the Montana Tax Appeal Board and then district court. One trap: to keep any refund alive, you must file a written protest with the treasurer and pay the disputed amount on time. Cascade County's protest form is due before the first Monday in June, or within 30 days of a classification notice or review decision.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Cascade County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Back taxes on real estate turn into a lien that the treasurer enforces. On a mobile home, the treasurer can instead go for a writ of execution, although the owner is normally offered a chance to pay everything or enter a payment program first.

With a house, the easy route is to sell and let the sale pay it off. The title company looks up the tax record and deducts any overdue tax, penalty and interest when funds are distributed. A cash buyer makes this smoother because no lender is waiting to approve the payoff.

In practice: ask the treasurer's office what you owe today, hand that figure to the title company, then read the closing statement and confirm the tax line matches before you sign.

One more Cascade County habit worth having: if a Great Falls buyer asks why your bill looks different from a neighbor's, the answer is usually the homestead class or the districts at the address, not an error. Point them to the classification notice and the mill levies on the statement.

Frequently asked questions

Who handles property tax bills in Cascade County?

The county treasurer's office sends the bill and takes payment. Appraised value and assessment appeals belong to the Montana Department of Revenue.

Can I spread my Cascade County tax over seven payments?

Yes, for a primary residence, once you file the county's application. Each installment is one-seventh of the bill and falls on the last day of the month from November 30 through May 31, under Montana Code 15-16-122.

What is the penalty for late property tax in Montana?

Delinquent tax draws interest at 5/6 of 1 percent per month and a 2 percent penalty. Taxes are delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 30 for the first half and after 5 p.m. on May 31 for the second half.

Does a buyer keep my homestead tax rate?

Not automatically. The rate stays on the property through the end of the calendar year of the sale, and the new owner must submit a homestead application to keep it for the next year.

Can I sell my Cascade County house for cash if taxes are owed?

Yes. Unpaid taxes, penalty and interest come out of the proceeds at closing, and the title company confirms the amount with the county treasurer.

Selling in Ravalli County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Ravalli County?

Ravalli County at a glance

The Bitterroot Valley makes up Ravalli County, tucked into western Montana below Missoula County and against the Idaho line. Hamilton is its one city. Darby, Pinesdale and Stevensville are the towns, and Corvallis, Florence, Victor, Conner and Sula round out the map. Public land covers a big share, with parts of the Bitterroot and Lolo National Forests inside the line.

The valley keeps growing: 44,174 people in 2020, and an estimate of 48,582 for 2025. With 84.4 percent of residents in rural areas, plenty of sellers live well outside the towns, and for them the treasurer and the state revenue office matter more than any city hall. Owners occupy 76.5 percent of occupied homes, and 11.0 percent of the 21,062 housing units stand vacant.

Wildfire risk and your sale

No other Montana county currently carries a higher wildfire risk to structures than Ravalli, and over 7,000 homes and structures sit at risk in the greater Bitterroot Front project area. That Forest Service project runs along the mountain front above the main valley, from McClain Creek in the north to Trapper Creek in the south, and relies on thinning, harvest and prescribed burning to cut fuel. Pockets of dense trees killed by mountain pine beetle, Douglas-fir bark beetle and western spruce budworm make the picture worse.

Near the forest edge, buyers will bring up fire risk and insurance. A cash buyer who takes the house as is keeps that talk brief. Whatever route you choose, have your insurance paperwork and any brush clearing records on hand.

Treasurer or state: who handles what

Worth and class come from the state's Department of Revenue. Bills, payments and delinquencies belong to the Ravalli County Treasurer. Send valuation questions to the first and payment problems to the second.

Montana splits the bill into equal halves. The deadline for half one is 5 p.m. on November 30, and half two follows at 5 p.m. on May 31 of the next year. Paying everything in November is allowed.

Payment eventRule
First installment5 p.m., November 30
Second installment5 p.m., May 31
Penalty and interest2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest per month (MCA 15-16-102)
Delinquent listPrinted each June, with notice that a tax lien is about to attach
Redemption window3 years after the lien attaches

Some 2026 due dates were moved, so check the date printed on your own bill with the Ravalli County Treasurer rather than assuming November 30.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Ravalli County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The 2026 tax rates

Four slices of value apply to a primary residence or long-term rental in 2026, each with a different percentage:

  • Value through $378,000: 0.76%.
  • $378,001 through $756,000: 0.90%.
  • $756,001 through $1,511,999: 1.10%.
  • $1,512,000 or more: 1.90%.

Cabins and other second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots all pay one flat 1.90%. On land, the rates are 2.05% for qualified agricultural land, 14.35% for non-qualified agricultural land and 0.37% for forest land, while a house and one-acre homesite on those parcels get the residential rate when lived in or rented long term. Qualifying means living there 7 or more months of 2026, or renting for 28 or more days at a time over at least 7 months.

Someone buying your house as a cabin will pay the flat rate, so your owner-occupied bill is not a safe preview of theirs.

Land adds a wrinkle. A listing with acreage should start with a look at how each parcel is classed, because agricultural, forest and residential land carry very different rates. A house and its one-acre homesite keep the residential rate only while someone lives there or rents it long term, which means the next owner's plans move the tax figure.

Appealing your value

Your first move is a form: AB-26, sent to the Department of Revenue to ask for an informal review. You have 30 days counted from the date printed on the classification and appraisal notice. Values for the 2025 to 2026 cycle reflect January 1, 2024.

Skipping the informal step is allowed. Take the case to the county tax appeal board by filing with the county clerk and recorder, still inside that 30-day span. The county commissioners appoint this board, and it answers to no one at the Department of Revenue. Losing there leaves the Montana Tax Appeal Board and finally district court.

Do not stop paying during the dispute. Under 15-1-402, MCA, a protest counts only when it is in writing, filed with the county treasurer, and the disputed tax is paid by its due date. Miss either and a lowered value will not earn you a refund.

Good exhibits: your own value estimate for that date, a sale price within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales, or a builder's cost breakdown.

Preparing a Bitterroot Valley listing

Start a folder with the latest tax bill, the classification and appraisal notice, any AB-26 or protest filings, and proof of homestead status, since buyers and the title company will want them. If the house is outside Hamilton or the small towns, which describes most of the valley, tell buyers early which taxing districts apply, since the county treasurer sends one bill and the state decides the class. Buyers who see a clean paper trail tend to move faster, and a cash buyer will usually close once the title work is clear.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ravalli County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If tax is owed when you sell

What you owe does not disappear when you sign a contract. Early in the August after an unpaid year, the debt becomes a lien, and nothing lifts it until every dollar of tax, interest, penalties and costs is paid. The county may keep it or sell it to an outside buyer, who receives an assignment certificate.

For three years after the lien attaches you keep title and can redeem by paying in full. Beyond that point, the holder can ask for a tax deed, and the property goes to public auction with opening bids at everything owed plus part of the appraised value.

A sale can still go through. At closing the title company pays the balance from your proceeds, and the deed is recorded with the county clerk and recorder alongside a Realty Transfer Certificate. Some owners can get help before it comes to that: the Property Tax Assistance Program for low-income Montanans, the Montana Disabled Veteran program and a land value assistance program for long-held family homes.

If you are behind, try this order: get the total from the treasurer, show the title company any lien notice that came in the mail, and request the payoff in writing before accepting an offer. Find out whether the lien was assigned to an investor, because that changes who receives the money.

Frequently asked questions

When are Ravalli County property taxes due?

The statute says 5 p.m. on November 30 for the first half and 5 p.m. on May 31 for the second. A few counties shifted their 2026 first-half dates, so ask the Ravalli County Treasurer what your bill says.

Who sets the value of my Ravalli County home?

The state does, through the Department of Revenue. The treasurer takes the figure on your classification and appraisal notice and builds your bill from it.

How long do I have to appeal my valuation?

Thirty days, counted from the date on your classification and appraisal notice. In that time file Form AB-26 with the Department of Revenue, or go straight to the county tax appeal board via the clerk and recorder.

What happens if I do not pay on time?

You owe a 2 percent penalty and 5/6 of 1 percent interest monthly. The debt becomes a lien, and once three years pass the lien holder can pursue a tax deed and a public auction.

Can I sell a Ravalli County house that has back taxes?

Yes. Since the lien stays with the property, it gets paid or settled at closing. A cash buyer can take the house as is, and the balance comes out of your proceeds.

Flathead County at a glance

Kalispell is the seat of Flathead County, a big northwest Montana county that runs north to the Canadian border. The 2020 census counted 104,357 people. Columbia Falls, Kalispell and Whitefish are the incorporated cities, and communities such as Bigfork, Lakeside, Somers, Martin City, Hungry Horse and West Glacier sit outside them.

One county name covers very different houses: in-town Kalispell homes, lakeshore places near Lakeside and Bigfork, and forested acreage close to Glacier National Park. Healthcare and tourism drive the local economy, and the park and the lake bring seasonal visitors. That produces a mix of second homes and vacation rentals alongside primary residences, and Montana taxes those two groups very differently.

Hospital and clinic workers also look for homes in the valley, and sellers who relocate for work often arrive with tight dates. That is one reason cash sales appeal to them.

Whether the house is a Kalispell in-town home or a lake property, two questions shape the sale: what tax class applied to it, and whether any tax is unpaid. The sections below cover both, and also what the buyer should expect once they take over the bill.

Wildfire and your sale

Fire risk comes up in Flathead County sales. The Wildfire Risk to Communities project rates the county's wildfire risk as very high, above 92 percent of U.S. counties. A 2021 Community Wildfire Protection Plan covers the wildland urban interface, the places where homes meet burnable vegetation.

For a house in the forested parts of the county, a buyer or an insurer may ask about defensible space, roofing and access for fire crews. Before a showing:

  • Clear dry vegetation and woodpiles from around the house.
  • Keep records of any fuels reduction work done on the lot.
  • Get a written statement of your current coverage from your insurer, because buyers will ask.

2026 tax rates by use of the property

Montana rewards owner occupancy. If you live in the house, or rent it long term, the first $378,000 of value is taxed at 0.76 percent, the next slice up to $756,000 at 0.90 percent, the next up to $1,511,999 at 1.10 percent, and anything beyond at 1.90 percent. Second homes, VRBOs, Airbnbs and cabins, plus vacant residential lots, pay 1.90 percent on the whole value. Mills for your district turn the taxable value into a bill.

In a county full of lake and park properties, that gap matters when you sell.

Use of the property2026 rate on the portion of value
Principal residence, first $378,0000.76 percent
Principal residence, $378,001 to $756,0000.90 percent
Principal residence, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10 percent
Second home, short-term rental, cabin1.90 percent flat
Residence on qualified agricultural land that is not a primary residence1.35 percent flat

If you rented the house short term, tell the buyer which rate applied to you. A buyer who plans to live there can enroll in the homestead program, but the new owner must submit an application by March 1 to keep the reduced rate the following year.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Flathead County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where to pay and what the bill looks like

The Flathead County Property Tax Office at 290 A North Main Street in Kalispell prepares and mails the bills, takes payments and works with the state on valuation. Bills go to the last known address at least 30 days before the November 30 due date, and the online portal shows 2026 real estate bills. The office phone is (406) 758-5680.

Paying online by debit or credit card adds a 3 percent fee. An eCheck is free. Search the portal with your assessor number only.

Delinquency timeline and tax liens

Here is how the calendar runs for an unpaid bill:

  • November 30: first half due. December 1: first half becomes delinquent.
  • May 31: second half due. June 1: second half becomes delinquent.
  • Late June: notice of a pending tax lien is published.
  • Early August: the lien is attached to delinquent properties. The treasurer must attach it no later than the first working day in August once notice has been given.

On top of the tax, you owe interest of 5/6 of 1 percent monthly and a one-time 2 percent penalty on the unpaid balance. A lien does not take your house on the spot, but it starts a legal process. Lien certificates can be assigned to a purchaser who pays the exact delinquent amount, so it is smart to clear taxes before you sell.

What if the valuation looks wrong?

Begin with the Montana Department of Revenue. It determines taxable value, including appraisal, classification, reductions and exemptions, and its Flathead County number is (406) 758-5700. Once you have the classification and appraisal notice, you get 30 days to file Form AB-26 for an informal review, or to file with the county clerk and recorder for a county tax appeal board hearing.

The county's protest form is meant only for use after an active appeal with the department. In writing, you protest to the county treasurer, and you pay the disputed tax when it is due. Skip either and a later reduction may not bring you a refund with interest. The Montana Tax Appeal Board and then district court are the later steps.

To make your case, bring comparable sales close to the January 1, 2024 valuation date, a fee appraisal or your own value estimate, among other items.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Flathead County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with back taxes or a lien

You can sell a house that has unpaid tax. The title company asks the treasurer's office for the payoff, deducts it from your proceeds, and the lien is released as part of closing. Allow time for that payoff request, since interest keeps accruing until the day funds are sent.

A cash purchase suits houses with deferred repairs or back taxes because the buyer takes the property as is and no lender has to approve the file. Before you accept an offer, ask for the closing statement in advance so you can see the tax line.

A simple order of events for a seller with an open balance:

  • Look up your bill on the county portal and note which halves are paid.
  • Call the property tax office with questions about the amount or a pending lien notice.
  • Give the title company the exact figure so it can request a payoff to the closing date.
  • Check the final statement to confirm the treasurer receives the full balance.

If you used a different rate class than the buyer will, such as a short-term rental, say so in writing so the buyer's tax estimate is based on the right class.

Frequently asked questions

How can I pay Flathead County property tax online?

Use the county's online tax portal. A debit or credit card adds a 3 percent fee, while an eCheck has no fee. Enter only your assessor number to search.

Is wildfire risk high in Flathead County?

Yes. The Wildfire Risk to Communities project rates it higher than 92 percent of U.S. counties. Insurance and defensible space often come up in a sale.

What is the Flathead County second-half tax deadline?

May 31, with delinquency beginning June 1. Interest then runs at 5/6 of 1 percent monthly plus a 2 percent penalty.

Will a tax lien take my Flathead County house?

A lien alone does not take the property. It is the county's claim for unpaid tax, penalty and interest, and it can be assigned to a purchaser who pays the delinquent amount. Paying the balance before or at closing clears it.

Can I sell a Flathead County house as is for cash?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house with deferred repairs or back taxes, and the title company pays the tax from your proceeds.
